terms.meaning: AES with a 256-bit key in Galois/Counter Mode; a workhorse AEAD in TLS, IPsec and SSH.
Current TLS 1.3 spec, published Jul 2026; obsoletes RFC 8446 and RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2).
2014 OpenSSL Heartbeat extension bug that let remote peers read process memory, private keys included.
2014 padding-oracle attack on SSL 3.0 CBC mode; the break that retired SSL 3.0 (RFC 7568).
SHA-1 has had practical collisions since 2017; NIST retires it by 31 Dec 2030 in favor of SHA-2 and SHA-3.
MD5 is collision-broken; RFC 6151 rules it out wherever collision resistance is required.
Classic image of a penguin encrypted in ECB mode whose outline stays visible: why ECB leaks patterns.
Field maxim: use vetted libraries and standard constructions instead of inventing ciphers or protocols.
Stock names for the two honest parties in protocol descriptions; Eve eavesdrops, Mallory tampers.
German WWII rotor cipher machine; its breaking by Polish and British codebreakers shaped the war.
British WWII codebreaking center where Enigma and Lorenz cipher traffic was read.
Truly random key as long as the message, never reused; the classic cipher proven to give perfect secrecy.
A cryptosystem must stay secure even if everything except the key is public (1883).
Asymmetric crypto: a public key encrypts or verifies; the matching private key decrypts or signs.
A later long-term key compromise cannot expose past sessions; TLS 1.3 dropped static key exchange for it.
Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data: confidentiality and integrity in one primitive.
Keyed-hash message authentication code built on any hash function; also specified in FIPS 198-1.
256-bit member of the SHA-2 family defined in the Secure Hash Standard.
Certificate and CRL profile for the Internet PKI; the format behind every HTTPS certificate.
PEM armor line that opens a Base64-encoded X.509 certificate.
Widely deployed open-source TLS and general-purpose cryptography library and command-line toolkit.
GNU Privacy Guard: free OpenPGP implementation for encrypting and signing files and email.
Free, automated certificate authority that issues TLS certificates via the ACME protocol.
Unique random value added to each password before hashing so equal passwords yield different hashes.
Number used once; repeating one under the same key breaks stream ciphers and GCM.
Public-key algorithms built to resist quantum attacks; NIST's first standards are FIPS 203, 204 and 205.
Module-lattice key encapsulation (formerly Kyber), mid parameter set; FIPS 203 published 13 Aug 2024.
Record encrypted traffic today, decrypt it once a large quantum computer exists; drives PQC urgency.
Proof that a statement is true without revealing anything beyond its truth.
Cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator; using a weak PRNG instead is CWE-338.
Recovering secrets from timing, power, EM or cache behavior instead of breaking the math itself.
Community reminder that 'crypto' named this field long before cryptocurrency borrowed the word.
Adaptive password-hashing function (1999) with a tunable cost factor.
Error feedback on CBC padding validity that leaks plaintext; the flaw class behind POODLE-style breaks.
TLS 1.3 was republished as RFC 9846 in Jul 2026, obsoleting RFC 8446.
Hybrid PQ/T TLS 1.3 key-share group (4588): X25519 plus ML-KEM-768, defined in RFC 10024.
First of the five cipher suites in the TLS 1.3 spec (0x1301-0x1305) and the only mandatory one.
terms.reference: IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry; RFC 9846

terms.meaning: TLS 1.3 suite favored on devices without AES hardware: ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 MAC.
terms.reference: IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry; RFC 9846

terms.meaning: AEAD pairing the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 authenticator; obsoletes RFC 7539.
HMAC-based extract-and-expand key derivation function; the TLS 1.3 key schedule is built on it.
Primary variant of Argon2, the Password Hashing Competition winner; RFC 9106 makes it mandatory.
Elliptic-curve key agreement function on Curve25519, defined alongside X448 in RFC 7748.
EdDSA signatures over edwards25519; approved by NIST in FIPS 186-5.
The prime that defines Curve25519's field; the curve takes its name from it.
Module-lattice signature (formerly Dilithium), security category 3; FIPS 204 published 13 Aug 2024.
Stateless hash-based signatures standardized from SPHINCS+; conservative security, large signatures.
Falcon-based lattice signature: compact, but hard to implement in constant time. FIPS 206 not yet out.
terms.reference: NIST news, 13 Aug 2024 (names draft FIPS 206 / FN-DSA)

terms.meaning: Code-based KEM selected 11 Mar 2025 as a non-lattice backup to ML-KEM; its standard is still pending.
CRYSTALS-Kyber became ML-KEM in FIPS 203; CRYSTALS-Dilithium became ML-DSA in FIPS 204.
Stateful hash-based signatures (RFC 8554, RFC 8391); a one-time key must never be reused. Used for firmware.
NSA quantum-resistant suite (2022): ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, AES-256, SHA-384/512, plus LMS and XMSS.
Draft PQC transition: 112-bit quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms deprecated after 2030; all disallowed after 2035.
Dual_EC_DRBG was removed in SP 800-90A Rev. 1 (2015); Hash_DRBG, HMAC_DRBG and CTR_DRBG remain.
FIPS 140-2 validations stayed active until 21 Sep 2026; all such certificates are now on the CMVP Historical list.
First practical SHA-1 collision: two different PDFs with one hash, announced 23 Feb 2017.
2015 downgrade of TLS to 512-bit export-grade DHE, made practical by widely shared primes.
2016 attack that used SSLv2 support on a shared key to decrypt modern TLS sessions.
2016 birthday-bound attack on 64-bit block ciphers such as 3DES in long-lived TLS sessions.
2017: flawed key generation in an Infineon library produced factorable keys in TPMs and smartcards.
2022 Java SE ECDSA verification flaw that accepted blank signatures as valid.
2023 prefix-truncation attack on the SSH transport that bypasses integrity checks on early packets.
A Debian OpenSSL patch (2006-2008) gutted PRNG entropy, so the keys it generated were guessable.
Isogeny-based KEM from NIST round 4, broken in 2022 by a classical key-recovery attack.
Encrypted Client Hello (Mar 2026): encrypts the ClientHello so SNI and ALPN stay private.
TLS 1.3 early data: saves a round trip but is replayable, so only idempotent requests belong there.
TLS alert: the sender could not negotiate an acceptable set of security parameters.
The line OpenSSL's s_client prints when the server certificate chain validated.
Python's timing-safe comparison for MACs and tokens; avoids the early-exit timing leak of ==.
nginx directive (now its default) allowing only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, in line with RFC 8996 deprecating 1.0/1.1.
Default OpenSSH filename for an Ed25519 public key; safe to share, unlike its private twin.
Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm: the anchor weakness for MD5, DES, RC4 and kin.
A CBC initialization vector an attacker can predict, which undermines the confidentiality CBC is meant to give.
Constant drawn from something public, like digits of pi, to show no hidden trapdoor was chosen.
Wry name for obtaining keys by coercing people rather than breaking the math.
Field adage: cryptanalysis never regresses, so margins that look fine today shrink tomorrow.
Weakness of SHA-256-style hashes used as H(key || msg); HMAC and SHA-3 are immune.
Code whose timing does not depend on secret data; the cure for Observable Timing Discrepancy.
Scripted, witnessed, recorded generation or use of a root key, as for the DNSSEC root KSK.
Triple DES encryption is disallowed after 2023; its 64-bit block falls to Sweet32. AES is the replacement.
RFC 7465 prohibits RC4 in TLS; ChaCha20-Poly1305 is today's fast software-only choice.
NIST's algorithm status ladder; 'legacy use' covers processing data that is already protected.
Ability to swap algorithms and parameters without redesign; the prerequisite for PQC migration.
1993 US key-escrow encryption chip running Skipjack; abandoned after public backlash.
Cryptography Bill of Materials: an inventory of the algorithms, keys and certificates in a system.
Open project of test vectors that catch known pitfalls in cryptographic library implementations.
Portable, easy-to-use crypto library with misuse-resistant defaults, derived from NaCl.
Authenticate the ciphertext and reject a bad tag before any decryption; RFC 7366 defines it for TLS and DTLS.

spec.as: Encrypt, then MAC, and verify the tag before you decrypt.

terms.text: A hash is not a signature
terms.meaning: A bare hash has no key, so anyone can recompute it; who sent the bytes needs a MAC or a signature.

spec.as: A hash proves the bytes match, never who sent them.

terms.meaning: A fast hash lets attackers test guesses cheaply; password hashing calls for a memory-hard KDF such as Argon2id.

spec.as: Never derive a key from a password with a bare hash.

terms.meaning: Even a strong cipher fails when its key sits in a repository, a log or a plain file; HSMs, KMSs and vaults hold keys.

spec.as: A key is only as safe as the place it is stored.

terms.meaning: TLS GREASE value: clients send reserved codes like this so servers learn to ignore what they do not know (RFC 8701).
terms.reference: RFC 8701; IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry

terms.meaning: TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV: a signaling value in the cipher list that marks a downgrade retry, not a cipher suite (RFC 7507).
terms.reference: RFC 7507; IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry

terms.meaning: TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV: a signaling value for secure-renegotiation support, not a cipher suite (RFC 5746).
terms.reference: RFC 5746; IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry

terms.meaning: Latin e and Cyrillic ie look alike in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable (IDN homograph spoofing).
Latin p and Cyrillic er look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin c and Cyrillic es look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin i and Cyrillic Byelorussian-Ukrainian i look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Known-answer test: the SHA-256 digest of a zero-length message, first 96 bits shown.
Known-answer test: the SHA-1 digest of "abc", first 96 bits shown; SHA-1 is retired but the vector still checks parsers.
Known-answer test: the full MD5 digest of a zero-length message, from the RFC 1321 test suite.
Known-answer test: the SHA3-256 digest of a zero-length message, first 96 bits shown.
Known-answer test: HMAC-SHA-256 with the key "Jefe" over "what do ya want for nothing?", first 96 bits shown.
TLS alert: a certificate in the chain has expired or is not valid yet.
TLS alert: a record failed its integrity check; a fatal alert, and never sent for padding errors.
TLS alert: the chain is valid but the issuing certificate authority is not trusted.
Eric Hughes, A Cypherpunk's Manifesto (9 Mar 1993): privacy is defended by writing crypto software, not by asking.
Bruce Schneier, The Guardian, Sep 2013: sound cryptography holds; what fails is the code, keys and endpoints around it.
Eric Hughes, A Cypherpunk's Manifesto (1993): privacy is the power to reveal oneself selectively, unlike secrecy.
Legacy 128-bit evidence hash; no longer collision-resistant, so it is logged beside SHA-256, not alone.
Public-key cryptosystem by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman (1978), based on the difficulty of factoring; PKCS #1.
1976 key-agreement protocol by Diffie and Hellman: two parties derive a shared secret over an open channel.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm: signatures over elliptic curves, with a fresh secret number per message.
Public-key cryptography on the points of an elliptic curve over a finite field; short keys for the strength they give.
Quantum algorithm that factors integers and solves discrete logarithms in polynomial time; the threat behind PQC.
Value made with a private key that anyone can check with the public key, showing who signed and that the data is intact.
Public, append-only logs of issued TLS certificates, so anyone can spot a certificate a CA should not have issued.
2011 attack on the chained IVs of CBC mode in SSL and TLS 1.0 that let a man in the middle recover HTTPS plaintext.
2012 attack on TLS compression: watching length changes lets a man in the middle recover secret HTTP header values.
2013 CRIME-style attack on HTTP response compression: length changes let a man in the middle recover secrets in HTTPS.
Indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack: an attacker cannot tell which of two chosen messages was encrypted.
Indistinguishability under adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack; the usual goal for encryption, and the one ML-KEM targets.
